iGEM · Dry lab

Modeling

An engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 circuit for pMMR/MSS colorectal cancer, gated on hypoxia, lactate and quorum. Two questions: where other than a tumour does it switch on, and what dose would a therapeutic effect require.

What the model decided

Six things. Each is a decision the project took because of the number beside it, not a description of a simulation. Everything after this page is the working.

1 · Is the AND gate really a product of its two inputs? Yes — at the endpoint. The two-way interaction is zero within error at 24 h, and the gate predicts any held-out corner to within 2.2 %. At 6 and 9 h the same prediction is wrong by up to 4.4×. → Licensed the entire safety chapter to factorise the gate, and forbade extrapolating mid-course ON/OFF ratios§1.1,§4.1.

2 · Where, other than a tumour, does the circuit switch on? The colonic mucosa, at 21.85× — and only because the native lldPRD repressions hold the gut lumen off. On the designed arms alone, all three luminal sites sit below 1.0. → Found a bottleneck nobody had looked at: last cycle's site list had no lumen in it at all§2.1.

3 · Can we "improve" the lactate sensor by removing its glucose/anoxia repression? No — that would destroy the safety argument. Luminal discrimination falls from 87–228× to 0.87–2.28×. → 🔴 A design decision: do not swap in a de-repressed variant§2.3.

4 · Below what lesion size can the hypoxia arm not fire, for any parameters? ≈178 µm. Pure geometry, zero fitted parameters — and it lands inside the 160–200 µm bracket Thomlinson & Gray measured histologically in 1955. → The hardest safety statement in the project, and the only parameter an independent measurement confirms§2.2.

5 · Keep the SsrA degron or drop it? Keep. All three doses clear the decision threshold, and ClpXP saturation means the degron amplifies selectivity rather than merely damping output. → Settled a build question the raw biomass numbers alone would have answered backwards§2.4.

6 · What dose does a therapeutic effect need? The clinical indication is met below the lowest dose we tested; CT26 needs 1.3–1.8× the highest. But reaching a 150 µm micro-lesion costs 4.95× and leaves only 4.41× of the mucosa margin. → Set the dose target, and showed micrometastasis is not a dose problem — which is why §3.6 exists§3.4,§3.5.

Every number on this page is computed, not transcribed. The figures, the tables and the worked substitutions are generated from the code in this repository, and a test suite of 329 assertions pins each of them to the function that produces it — so the page cannot hold a stale number, and a reader who wants to check one can run it. §4 then puts the central claims through out-of-sample tests: held-out gate corners, held-out doses, and a 24 h capacity forecast built from truncated curves. All pass.

Two of these results changed our own minds, which is the part we would most like a reader to weigh. §2.5 records two inherited sensor parameters that turned out to have published measurements disagreeing with them; we adopted the measurements and recomputed every number here. §5.1 withdraws a selectivity index we had previously published, caught by our own consistency checking rather than by anyone objecting.

What we set out to answer

Two questions decide whether this design is worth building:

Safety — where, other than a tumour, does this circuit switch on?

Efficacy — what dose would a therapeutic effect require?

Everything below is organised under those two headings. We do not organise by length scale, because a micro/meso/macro split describes the model rather than the decision, and every section here exists to settle a decision.

The circuit:

How to read this page

Each section states the specific question it answers, then its governing equations with every symbol defined, then the parameters with their units and provenance, then the numbers substituted in, and only then the result. Where a limitation changes a conclusion we say so next to that conclusion, and §5 collects the rest.

  • Equation numbers run (1)…(N) in reading order. The source of this page tags each equation with its number in EQUATIONS.md instead, and the build emits the mapping to outputs/equation_index.md, so every formula here can still be traced to the function that evaluates it.
  • Evidence grades: calibration = fitted to our data · literature prior = measured by someone else on a comparable system · scenario = a value we declared · derived = computed from other entries · protocol = a threshold fixed before it was used. The literature-prior grade separates "somebody measured this" from "we picked this", which the first four grades ran together.
  • Full parameter census is in §6, generated from config/parameters.csv; src/parameters.py resolves each row against the constant the code actually uses and fails the test suite if the two disagree, so this page cannot hold a stale copy.

1. Calibration

1.0 What our wet lab measured, and what each measurement decides

Everything quantitative on this page is anchored to 391 measurements our own team ran this cycle, in four blocks. Nothing in this chapter is inherited and nothing in it is a literature value; the whole chapter is the wet lab's data and what it forces the model to say.

Table 2. The experimental blocks, and the decision each one settles.

Block What was measured Measurements What it decides
1–2OD₆₀₀ growth curves: 2 constructs (GSDMD, GSDMD–SsrA) × 4 conditions (21/1 % O₂ × 0/20 mM lactate) × 8 timepoints × 3 replicates192the carrying capacity $K$ at every site§2.1 and the chassis cost of the SsrA tag§2.4 — fitted in §1.3
3reporter fluorescence intensity: 4 corners × 4 timepoints × 3 replicates48the magnitude of the hypoxia contribution, 1.33×§1.2
4reporter percent-positive: 4 corners × 4 timepoints × 3 replicates48the AND-gate interaction test itself — the one result the entire safety chapter is factored on§1.1, and the held-out prediction that validates it§4.1
5co-culture killing, dose series: 7 constructs × 3 doses (6/8/10 OD) × 3 replicates, CT2662the dose–kill power law $b=2.651$, and through it every dose number in §3.4 and the whole safety-dose collision in §3.5
6co-culture killing, cell-line pairing: 7 constructs × 2 lines (CT26, L929) at 10 OD41the construct's own selectivity index, 3.3×§1.4

Read the last column: block 4 is what lets the gate be written as a product at all, and block 5 is what turns the model's safety margin into a dose in OD. Neither is replaceable by a literature value, because no published study used this construct.

Two measurements do more work than their cost suggests, and both are worth saying out loud:

  • Running both constructs in the same growth block is what makes the first-hour burst interpretable§1.3. The tagged strain is the control for the medium, so "lactate slows growth" is ruled out by the data rather than argued away.
  • Running block 5's seven constructs at the same three doses is what lets the killing be taken net of the gfp carrier§3.4, instead of crediting the effector with the chassis's own effect.

Where the data does not reach, we say so rather than filling the gap: §5.1 lists what this workbook does not contain, and §7 costs the experiments that would close each gap.

1.1 Is the AND gate multiplicative?

Question. Read as raw fluorescence the two inputs together give 227× where a multiplicative gate predicts 2768×. Is that 12× shortfall real sub-multiplicativity, or an artefact of a saturated readout? And once the artefact is removed, what does the data actually support?

This matters because every safety result below writes the gate as a product of three arms (Eq. (11)). This section is the measured basis for that factorisation.

Corners: A = 21 % O₂ · B = 1 % O₂ · C = 21 % + 20 mM lactate · D = 1 % + 20 mM.

Model

If per-cell log-expression is normal with condition-dependent mean $\mu$ and a common spread $\sigma$, and the cytometry gate is a fixed threshold $\theta$, the positive fraction is the standard probit model4:

$$p=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu-\theta}{\sigma}\right) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad z\equiv\Phi^{-1}(p)=\frac{\mu-\theta}{\sigma}$$
(1)

A fold change between two corners is then

$$\text{fold}=\exp(\sigma\,\Delta z)$$
(2)

$\theta$ cancels from any difference; $\sigma$ does not, and Eq. (2) depends on it exponentially.

A multiplicative gate means the two inputs are additive on $\mu$, hence additive in probit units, hence the two-way interaction vanishes:

$$I=z_D-z_C-z_B+z_A\ \overset{!}{=}\ 0$$
(3)
$$\mathrm{SE}(I)=\sqrt{\sum_{c\in\{A,B,C,D\}} s_c^2/n_c}$$
(4)

where

  • $\mu$ is the condition-dependent mean of per-cell log-expression.
  • $\sigma$ is the common spread of per-cell log-expression.
  • $\theta$ is the fixed cytometry threshold for gating positive cells.
  • $p$ is the positive fraction of cells above the cytometry gate.
  • $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution, and $\Phi^{-1}(\cdot)$ its inverse (the probit function).
  • $z$ is the probit-transformed positive fraction.
  • $\text{fold}$ is the fold change between two experimental corners.
  • $I$ is the two-way interaction term, zero for a multiplicative gate.
  • $\mathrm{SE}(I)$ is the standard error of $I$.
  • $z_A$, $z_B$, $z_C$, $z_D$ are the probit values of the four corners $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$.
  • $s_c^2$ and $n_c$ are the sample variance and sample size of corner $c$.

$\sigma$ scales every term in Eq. (3) equally, so it cancels from the test. That is why the interaction test is the load-bearing result and the fold magnitudes are decoration.

$\sigma$cell-to-cell spreadnot identifiable from this dataset—
$\sigma_{9.23}$spread reproducing last cycle's published folds2.53not a measurement
—multiplicativity criterion$I$ within $2\,\mathrm{SE}$ of zeroprotocol

At 3 h corner A reads 0 % positive, where $\Phi^{-1}$ diverges, so that timepoint cannot be inverted at all; our code raises rather than silently clipping, because clipping would fabricate a finite $z$.

Results

Time Oxygen $B{-}A$ Oxygen $D{-}C$ Lactate $C{-}A$ Lactate $D{-}B$ Interaction $t$
6 h0.7261.0100.8231.107+0.284 ± 0.2401.18
9 h0.5921.7271.1702.306+1.135 ± 0.3503.24
24 h1.1281.1172.5572.546−0.011 ± 0.157−0.07

At 24 h the two oxygen estimates agree to 0.98 % and the two lactate estimates to 0.43 %, and the interaction is zero within error. The oxygen effect is the same with and without lactate, and the lactate effect the same under normoxia and hypoxia — which is what additivity, and so multiplicativity, means. These are two independent internal checks rather than one fit.

At 9 h the interaction is significantly positive ($t=3.24$, 8 df, $p\approx0.01$): the gate is super-multiplicative while it is still turning on. This is consistent with hypoxia acting on rate rather than level — three readouts put the 24 h hypoxia increment at only 1.18–1.33×, where mid-course it is 3.4×. A pure rate effect shows up as apparent synergy in the transient and disappears once both corners saturate.

So the AND claim belongs to the endpoint. Mid-course ON/OFF ratios must not be extrapolated with a multiplicative model. §4.1 turns this from a test into an out-of-sample prediction.

The interaction test is the load-bearing result here; the fold magnitudes are decoration. $\sigma$ cancels from the test (Eq. (3)) but not from a fold, so we report the folds as σ-conditional and build nothing on them:

$\sigma$ Oxygen fold Lactate fold Implied population CV
1.03.1×12.9×131 %
2.5317.4×645×2,452 %
4.091.2×27,660×298,000 %

The last column is worth a line, because $\sigma$ and the coefficient of variation are the same statement for log-normal expression ($\mathrm{CV}=\sqrt{e^{\sigma^{2}}-1}$). The $\sigma$ that reproduces last cycle's published 17× and 642× implies a population spread of about 2,450 % — four decades of fluorescence. Possible for a strongly bimodal reporter, but it was never stated as a claim: it was fixed implicitly by inverting to the answer. We quote those two numbers only to say where they came from.

1.2 Lactate dominates the gate

Three readouts agree on how much the hypoxia input contributes at 24 h: positive fraction rises 1.18× (82.9 → 97.9 %), intensity 1.33× (253,571 → 337,332), and the untagged strain's endpoint OD₆₀₀ not at all (1.380 → 1.380). Mid-course, at 6 h and 9 h, hypoxia multiplies the positive fraction by 3.4×.

Lactate is necessary and close to sufficient; hypoxia sets how fast the gate opens, not whether it opens. This is why §2.3's luminal lactate load is close to the whole safety story.

1.3 Growth and carrying capacity

Question. Growth curves jump in the first hour and then creep, and no three-parameter sigmoid fits both phases. Where exactly is the misfit, is the first-hour burst real growth or a plate artefact, and does the misfit propagate into any conclusion we use?

Model

Two candidate laws, chosen so their structures differ diagnostically:

$$N(t)=K\exp\!\big(-b\,e^{-ct}\big)$$
(5)
$$N(t)=K-(K-N_0)e^{-kt}$$
(6)

Eq. (5) is the Gompertz form in the parameterisation standard for bacterial growth curves5. It has its maximum rate at an interior inflection; Eq. (6) has it at $t=0$. If the data's maximum rate is at $t=0$, the former structurally cannot fit it.

$$J=\frac{\mathrm{RMSE}_{\text{with }t=0}}{\mathrm{RMSE}_{\,t\ge1\text{h}}}$$
(7)
$$B=\frac{v_{0\to1}(\text{induced})}{v_{0\to1}(\text{uninduced})}$$
(8)
$$K=\bar y_{24},\qquad \text{half-width}=t_{0.975,2}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n},\qquad t_{0.975,2}=4.3027$$
(9)

where

  • $N(t)$ is the bacterial density (OD₆₀₀) at time $t$.
  • $K$ is the carrying capacity, taken as the measured 24 h mean OD.
  • $N_0$ is the initial inoculum density.
  • $b$, $c$ are the Gompertz shape parameters.
  • $k$ is the first-order approach rate (h⁻¹).
  • $J$ is the ratio of the fit error with the $t=0$ point included to the fit error from 1 h on.
  • $\mathrm{RMSE}$ is the root-mean-square error of the fitted growth curve.
  • $v_{0\to1}$ is the growth velocity over the first hour (OD h⁻¹).
  • $B$ is the first-hour growth-burst ratio, induced over uninduced.
  • $\bar y_{24}$ is the mean 24 h OD across replicate measurements.
  • $s$ and $n$ are the sample standard deviation and the number of replicate measurements.
  • $t_{0.975,2}$ is the 97.5th percentile of Student's $t$ distribution with 2 degrees of freedom (4.3027).

Substituting and results

The three normoxic corners improve 5.6–7.4×; the anaerobic corners do not move — they have no burst to misfit. Freeing the initial condition (Eq. (6)) does not help (0.1331 vs 0.1469, a 10 % gain, with fitted $N_0$ only 1.16–1.23), so the problem is the shape of the first hour, not the anchor value.

The burst is real growth. Same medium, same oxygen, different construct:

Construct Condition induced $v_{0\to1}$ uninduced $B$
GSDMD-SsrAaerobic + lactate0.63670.81000.786
GSDMDaerobic + lactate0.10670.82670.129
GSDMD-SsrAanaerobic + lactate0.47670.49330.966
GSDMDanaerobic + lactate0.08000.46670.171

A plate artefact would not know which measurements came from which construct. This one does: the tagged strain keeps 79–97 % of its first-hour burst and the self-toxic one keeps 13–17 %. The tagged construct serves as a control for the medium itself, ruling out "lactate slows growth".

This also sharpens the self-toxicity phenotype from "42 % less biomass at 24 h" to "the first-hour growth burst is abolished by 83–87 %".

The misfit does not propagate. Every downstream use takes a measured 24 h value — site densities in §2.1, the chassis-cost anchor in §2.4 — and nothing in this project reads a value off a fitted curve. We assert this executably (misfit_propagates() -> False), so if any module ever starts using fitted trajectories the test suite fails.

What does propagate is the capacity itself, determined to 1.05 %–15.23 % (tight normoxic, wider anaerobic). The tissue axis consumes ratios of these, so the precision is ample.

1.4 Construct selectivity

Pairing within a single experiment, the construct we build kills CT26 at 4.77 % and L929 at 1.43 % at 10 OD — a selectivity index of 3.3× ($p<0.001$, $n=3$). Figures of 11.4× and 2.97× quoted earlier paired a numerator from one block with a denominator from another and are withdrawn§5.1.

This is the one number on the page that nothing downstream depends on, and that is by design. 3.3× is modest, and an AND gate exists precisely so that it does not have to be large: the safety argument in chapter 2 is carried entirely by the circuit's tissue selectivity — 21.85× at the bottleneck from the sensors, before the effector contributes anything at all — rather than by any intrinsic preference of GSDMD-N for tumour cells. A design that needed the effector to be selective would be a worse design.

That matters for how the measurement should be read. The pair is a mouse colon carcinoma against a mouse fibroblast line, CT26.WT6 and NCTC clone 929 / L-9297, which differ in tissue of origin as well as in malignancy. So 3.3× is "tumour line over a normal line", not "colon tumour over colon epithelium". We report it as the former and use it as neither: §3.5's off-target argument is built on gate output and crypt renewal, not on this ratio.

2. Safety — where else does the gate switch on?

2.1 The tissue axis

Question. With the gut lumen added to the site list, what is the gate output at each normal site relative to the tumour, and which site is the bottleneck? Is the "22–910×" range we inherited a measurement uncertainty or the span of one unidentified parameter?

Model

Both designed sensors are Hill functions with a basal floor — the lactate arm activated by its stimulus, the hypoxia arm repressed by oxygen:

$$f_L(L)=b_L+(1-b_L)\frac{L^{n_L}}{EC_{50}^{n_L}+L^{n_L}}, \qquad f_O(C)=b_O+(1-b_O)\frac{K_{O_2}^{n_O}}{K_{O_2}^{n_O}+C^{n_O}}$$
(10)

Because LuxI sits under pPepT, the quorum signal is proportional to hypoxia activity times density, $Q\propto f_O N$. Gate output at a site relative to the tumour core is therefore

$$R_{\text{margin}}(\text{site})= \underbrace{\frac{f_L(L_t)}{f_L(L_s)}}_{\text{lactate arm}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{f_O(C_t)}{f_O(C_s)}}_{\text{hypoxia arm}} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{f_O(C_t)/f_O(C_s)}{N_s/N_t}\right)^{n_Q}}_{\text{quorum arm}} \cdot \underbrace{\rho_{\text{anox}}\rho_{\text{glu}}}_{\text{native repression}}$$
(11)

Setting $R_{\text{margin}}=1$ and solving for the luminal density ratio $d=N_s/N_t$ gives a critical density:

$$d_{\text{crit}}=\text{hyp}\cdot\big(\text{lac}\cdot\text{hyp}\cdot R_{\text{rep}}\big)^{1/n_Q}, \qquad R_{\text{rep}}=\rho_{\text{anox}}^{-1}\rho_{\text{glu}}^{-1}$$
(12)

where

  • $f_L(L)$ is the lactate-arm activity, a Hill function of lactate with a basal floor (Eq. (10)).
  • $f_O(C)$ is the hypoxia-arm activity, a Hill function repressed by oxygen (Eq. (10)).
  • $L$ and $C$ are the lactate concentration (mM) and the oxygen concentration (% O₂).
  • $b_L$, $n_L$ and $EC_{50}$ are the lactate-arm basal fraction, Hill coefficient and half-maximal lactate concentration (1/7, 1.0, 1.6 mM).
  • $b_O$, $n_O$ and $K_{O_2}$ are the hypoxia-arm basal fraction, Hill coefficient and half-maximal repression oxygen (0.05, 2.0, 0.49 % O₂).
  • $Q$ is the quorum signal, proportional to hypoxia activity times bacterial density.
  • $N$ is the bacterial density (relative OD), assigned from the measured capacities of §1.3.
  • $R_{\text{margin}}(\text{site})$ is the gate output at a site relative to the tumour core.
  • $n_Q$ is the quorum Hill coefficient (1.0 published, swept 0.95–1.5).
  • $\rho_{\text{anox}}$ and $\rho_{\text{glu}}$ are the residual activities of the native anoxic and glucose repressions (0.1 each).
  • $d=N_s/N_t$ is the luminal density ratio, and $d_{\text{crit}}$ its critical value at which $R_{\text{margin}}=1$.
  • $\text{hyp}=f_O(C_t)/f_O(C_s)$ and $\text{lac}=f_L(L_t)/f_L(L_s)$ are the hypoxia- and lactate-arm ratios.
  • $R_{\text{rep}}=\rho_{\text{anox}}^{-1}\rho_{\text{glu}}^{-1}$ is the native-repression product.
  • Subscripts $t$ and $s$ denote the tumour core and the site.

Note the scaling: the margin repression buys grows only as $R_{\text{rep}}^{1/n_Q}$, so a strong repression is worth less when the quorum arm is steep.

The quorum arm is treated as sub-threshold, i.e. the tumour sits below the quorum set point. This is inherited rather than invented: if the tumour were saturated the arm would contribute no selectivity at all, and neither the tissue folds nor the lesion-size turn-on of §2.2 could arise.

Adding the native repressions (100× combined, acting only at the anoxic glucose-rich luminal sites) moves the healthy lumen to 60.5×, faecal to 28.7× and dysbiotic to 23.1×, while leaving the mucosa at 21.85× untouched. So the native repression does not merely help the lumen — it changes which site is the weakest link:

Bottleneck Margin
Without repressiondysbiotic lumen0.231× (unsafe)
With repressioncolonic mucosa21.85× (safe)

Note that all three luminal sites are now unambiguously below 1.0 without the native repression, where the inherited priors left the healthy lumen marginal at 1.21×. The published oxygen affinity makes the designed circuit's luminal problem worse, and the native repression correspondingly more load-bearing.

The "22–910×" range is a span of $n_Q$, not a measurement uncertainty. Last cycle's two calibrations shared every fixed prior and differed almost entirely in that one coefficient ($n_Q=1.000$ and $2.978$). Sweeping it, now against the published value rather than last cycle's:

$n_Q$ Colonic mucosa Well-perfused
0.9520.7×93.2×
1.0 (published centre)21.9×101.7×
1.5 (published upper)37.0×242×
2.0 (9.23's prior)62.6×578×
3.0179×3,285×
4.0513×18,671×

An exogenous-AHL dose response on pLux would pin $n_Q$ down in an afternoon.

⚠️ Honest caveat. The reconstructed span over $n_Q\in[1,4]$ (mucosa 10.1–74.4×) does not cover the published 22.3–909.6×. This model is a homogeneous point estimate where last cycle solved a spatially averaged PDE, so we claim agreement in direction and driver, not reproduction.

Last cycle's lactate priors were considerably more generous than the published characterisation of the part we actually chose ($EC_{50}$ 5.0 vs 1.6 mM, $n_L$ 2.0 vs 1.0, basal 0.0078 vs ≈1/7 — all three shifted toward better discrimination, none anchored to BBa_M36021). That inflated the lactate arm by 5.23× at the mucosa and 14.48× at the healthy lumen. But at the dysbiotic lumen the inflation factor is 0.83× — the generous prior is actually worse, because at 100 mM both priors saturate. Safety cannot be bought by changing priors; the correction matters because it stops us telling a flattering story, not because it changes the verdict.

The one remaining free parameter is luminal EcN density. Eq. (12) gives

$d_{\text{crit}}=0.5154\times(0.8689\times0.5154\times100)^{1/1}=\mathbf{23.08}$

with repression, against 0.231 without: the lumen stays off as long as luminal EcN density does not exceed roughly 23× the tumour's. At $n_Q=1$ the critical density scales linearly in the repression fold rather than as its square root, which is why this threshold is three times what the inherited prior gave.

There is one human measurement bearing on that threshold, and it is a warning as much as a reassurance. In a double-blind trial, patients took 10⁹ CFU of EcN daily for 14 days before resection; tumour tissue was enriched for EcN over matched normal tissue ($p=0.03$), but two of the six treated participants carried comparably high EcN in adjacent normal colon and showed no tumour enrichment at all1. Six patients cannot give a distribution for $d$, and we do not treat them as one. What they do establish is that $d>1$ happens in people — so the sweep to $d=10$ is covering a real case, not a hypothetical one, and the 23.08 threshold is the number to watch.

2.2 Lesion size: a floor that needs no calibration

Question. Below what radius can the hypoxia arm not leave basal for any parameter values? And is the inherited "14×–6891×" size turn-on the same uncertainty as §2.1's, or independent evidence?

Model

Oxygen penetrates a fixed depth $d_{O_2}$ from the perfused surface, so

$$r_{\text{core}}(R)=\max(R-d_{O_2},0), \qquad \phi_{\text{hyp}}(R)=\left(\frac{r_{\text{core}}(R)}{R}\right)^{3}$$
(13)
$$\bar f_O(R)=\phi_{\text{hyp}}f_O(C_{\text{core}})+(1-\phi_{\text{hyp}})f_O(C_{\text{rim}})$$
(14)
$$G(R)=\Big[\bar f_O(R)\cdot\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)\Big]^{n_Q}$$
(15)

where $\Psi_{\text{centre}}$ is the closed-form AHL volume-integration kernel of §3.2 (Eq. (35)) — no PDE solve is needed. The two mechanisms separate cleanly before the Hill exponent is applied:

$$\underbrace{\frac{\bar f_O(R_2)}{\bar f_O(R_1)}}_{\text{hypoxic volume}}\times \underbrace{\frac{\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R_2)}{\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R_1)}}_{\text{AHL integration}} =\frac{Q(R_2)}{Q(R_1)}$$
(16)

And a direct corollary of Eq. (13), with no sensor parameter in it at all:

$$R<d_{O_2}\ \Longrightarrow\ \phi_{\text{hyp}}\equiv0\ \Longrightarrow\ \bar f_O\equiv f_O(C_{\text{rim}})=\text{const}$$
(17)

where

  • $R$ is the lesion radius (µm).
  • $d_{O_2}$ is the oxygen penetration depth from the perfused surface (178 µm, from the 1 % O₂ contour at 222 µm in a 400 µm nodule).
  • $r_{\text{core}}(R)=\max(R-d_{O_2},0)$ is the hypoxic-core radius.
  • $\phi_{\text{hyp}}(R)=(r_{\text{core}}/R)^3$ is the hypoxic volume fraction.
  • $f_O(C)$ is the hypoxia-arm Hill function of Eq. (10).
  • $\bar f_O(R)$ is the volume-averaged hypoxia-arm activity.
  • $C_{\text{core}}$ and $C_{\text{rim}}$ are the oxygen concentrations at the lesion core and rim (0.5 % and 5 %).
  • $\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)$ is the normalised AHL at the lesion centre (Eq. (35)).
  • $n_Q$ is the quorum Hill coefficient.
  • $Q(R)$ is the quorum signal for a lesion of radius $R$.
  • $G(R)$ is the gate output for a lesion of radius $R$.

Substituting

$d_{O_2}$ is calibrated to last cycle's own statement that the 1 % O₂ contour sits at 222 µm in a 400 µm nodule, i.e. $400-222=\mathbf{178\ \mu m}$.

At $R=150$ µm: $r_{\text{core}}=0$, so $\bar f_O=f_O(5\,\%)=0.059037$, independent of $R$. At $R=400$ µm: $\phi_{\text{hyp}}=(222/400)^3=0.170954$ and

$$\bar f_O(400)=0.170954\times0.515405+0.829046\times0.059037=\mathbf{0.137055}$$

Results

A lesion below ≈178 µm has no hypoxic volume whatsoever, so the hypoxia arm cannot leave basal however the circuit is parameterised. This is pure geometry — zero fitted parameters — and it is the hardest safety statement in this work.

The floor agrees with a seventy-year-old histological measurement

Our 178 µm comes from last cycle's own oxygen contour, with no histology in it. It is worth checking against the measurement the whole field's diffusion distance comes from. Thomlinson and Gray sectioned human lung carcinomas and found that the radius of intact tumour cells surrounding a necrotic core never exceeded 180 µm; central necrosis was absent in every section below 160 µm radius and present in every section above 200 µm12,13.

That is a measured bracket for exactly the quantity $d_{O_2}$ represents, and our independently derived value falls inside it, 1 % below its upper edge:

$d_{O_2}$ Source Floor $\phi_{\text{hyp}}(400\ \mu m)$ 150→1000 µm turn-on
160 µmhistology, necrosis absent below160 µm0.2160$2.07\times10^{-5}$
178 µmour oxygen contour178 µm0.1710$2.31\times10^{-5}$
200 µmhistology, necrosis present above200 µm0.1250$2.63\times10^{-5}$

The floor is $d_{O_2}$ by construction, so the histological bracket transfers to it directly: the smallest lesion that can develop a hypoxic core is 160–200 µm, and 178 µm is our reading inside that range. Across the whole bracket the 150→1000 µm turn-on moves by 27 %, which changes nothing — the statement being made is that small lesions have no hypoxic volume, and where that threshold sits is bounded by histology rather than by our circuit.

This is the only parameter in the project where an independent measurement lands on a value we derived from somewhere else entirely. We flag it because the reverse — a derived number that the literature contradicts — is what §2.5 found for the oxygen affinity, and a reader is entitled to know which is which.

Decomposing the 150 → 1000 µm turn-on by Eq. (16):

Mechanism Fold
Hypoxic volume (mean pPepT activity)5.293×
AHL volume integration36.907×
Combined quorum signal195.4×

The AHL term carries 6.5× the weight of the hypoxia term — the size switch is fundamentally a volume integrator, which §3.2 reaches independently.

Applying only $n_Q$ to last cycle's own signal fold of 22× reproduces its published range: $22^{1.000}=22.0$ against 14.1, and $22^{2.978}=9948$ against 6891 — both within 1.6× across three orders of magnitude.

The tissue-axis range (22–910×) and the size range (14–6891×) are the same unidentified Hill coefficient propagating through a power law. They must not be presented as two independent pieces of evidence.

⚠️ Our free-field kernel has no boundary sink, giving a signal fold of 195.4× against last cycle's 22× — an overestimate of 9.47×, because its PDE imposed a Robin washout at the nodule surface that drains a large nodule's integration advantage. Use 22× when an absolute value is needed; use this section for the mechanism split and the geometric floor.

2.3 The colon lumen

Question. We dose orally, so the bacteria sit in the colon lumen first. Are the two designed arms anti-selective there — and can that be decided without the sensor parameters we cannot measure? If they are, what holds the lumen off, and how strong does it need to be?

Model

The lactate sensor's $EC_{50}$ and Hill coefficient are not identifiable from our data: the reporter experiment has two oxygen levels and two lactate levels, which locate neither a midpoint nor a slope, and the lactate gradient that would fix them will not be run this cycle. So we invert the question — for which sensor parameters is the lumen held off while the tumour is on? — and find that for both designed arms the parameters are not needed at all.

Both arms are monotone in their stimulus (Eq. (10)). Therefore

$$s_{\text{offsite}}\ge s_{\text{target}} \ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{f(s_{\text{target}})}{f(s_{\text{offsite}})}\le1 \quad\text{for every }(EC_{50},n,b)$$
(18)

with hypoxia stimulus expressed monotonically as $s_O=-C$.

The lactate arm also has an analytic ceiling. Pushing $EC_{50}$ far above both concentrations puts them on the initial power-law stretch $f_L\sim L^{n_L}$, so the ratio approaches $(L_t/L_{\text{off}})^{n_L}$ from below and never exceeds it; a non-zero basal level caps it again at $1/b_L$:

$$\sup_{EC_{50}}\frac{f_L(L_t)}{f_L(L_{\text{off}})} =\min\!\left\{\left(\frac{L_t}{L_{\text{off}}}\right)^{n_L},\ \frac{1}{b_L}\right\}$$
(19)
$$n_L\ \ge\ \frac{\ln R_{\text{req}}}{\ln(L_t/L_{\text{off}})}$$
(20)

The native repressions enter multiplicatively on the luminal side only:

$$R_{\text{margin}}=\frac{f_L(L_t)}{f_L(L_{\text{off}})\,\rho_{\text{anox}}\rho_{\text{glu}}}, \qquad \big(\rho_{\text{anox}}\rho_{\text{glu}}\big)^{-1}\ge\frac{R_{\text{req}}}{R_{\text{derepressed}}}$$
(21)

The one candidate among the designed inputs that is not structurally anti-selective is luminal washout:

$$\eta_{\text{ret}}=\frac{k_{\text{decay}}}{k_{\text{decay}}+k_{\text{wash}}}, \quad k_{\text{decay}}=\frac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}^{\text{AHL}}}, \quad k_{\text{wash}}=\frac{1}{\tau_{\text{transit}}}$$
(22)

where

  • $s_{\text{target}}$ and $s_{\text{offsite}}$ are the stimulus strength at the tumour and at an off-target site; for the hypoxia arm the stimulus is $s_O=-C$.
  • $f(s)$ is the sensor activity as a function of its stimulus.
  • $EC_{50}$, $n$ and $b$ are the sensor half-maximal stimulus, Hill coefficient and basal fraction.
  • $L_t$ is the tumour lactate concentration (8.0 mM).
  • $L_{\text{off}}$ is the off-target luminal lactate concentration (0.6–100 mM across the luminal scenarios).
  • $n_L$ and $b_L$ are the lactate-arm Hill coefficient and basal fraction (1.0, 1/7).
  • $R_{\text{req}}$ is the required margin (10× here).
  • $R_{\text{derepressed}}$ is the margin obtained without the native repressions.
  • $\rho_{\text{anox}}$ and $\rho_{\text{glu}}$ are the residual activities of the native anoxic and glucose repressions, entering multiplicatively on the luminal side only.
  • $\eta_{\text{ret}}$ is the fraction of AHL retained in the lumen.
  • $k_{\text{decay}}=\ln2/t_{1/2}^{\text{AHL}}$ is the AHL first-order decay rate, and $t_{1/2}^{\text{AHL}}$ the AHL half-life (8 h).
  • $k_{\text{wash}}=1/\tau_{\text{transit}}$ is the luminal washout rate, and $\tau_{\text{transit}}$ the colonic transit time (swept 1–24 h).

Parameters

Symbol Value Grade Source
$L_t$8.0 mMliterature priorthe median of the clinical series, ≈8 µmol g⁻¹14
$L_{\text{off}}$ healthy0.6 mMliterature priorrectal lumen by equilibrium dialysis, L-lactate 0.5 (0–1.6), D-lactate 0.1 (0–0.8) mM, $n=11$ healthy controls15
$L_{\text{off}}$ faecal5.0 mMliterature priorlactate < 5 mM in healthy faeces16
$L_{\text{off}}$ dysbiotic100 mMscenario onlyfaecal lactate to 110 mM in short bowel17, raised in active UC18
$C_{\text{off}}$0 %binary flaglumen anoxic — see §2.3.4
$t_{1/2}^{\text{AHL}}$8 hscenarioplaceholder
$\tau_{\text{transit}}$swept 1–24 hscenariocolonic transit is slow (24–72 h)

Substituting

With $n_L=1$, $EC_{50}=1.6$ mM, $b_L=1/7$:

$$f_L(8.0)=\tfrac17+\tfrac67\cdot\frac{8.0}{9.6}=\mathbf{0.857143}, \qquad f_L(0.6)=\tfrac17+\tfrac67\cdot\frac{0.6}{2.2}=\mathbf{0.376623}$$

giving 2.276× at the healthy lumen; likewise 1.082× at faecal lactate and 0.869× — already inverted — in dysbiosis.

Comparing stimuli site by site (Eq. (18)):

Site O₂ Lactate Lactate arm Hypoxia arm
Tumour core (target)0.5 %8 mM——
Colonic mucosa2 %1.5 mM✅ 1.54×✅ 3.38×
Well-perfused10 %1 mM✅ 1.81×✅ 13.63×
Colon lumen (healthy)0 %0.6 mM✅ 2.28×❌ anti-selective
Colon lumen (faecal)0 %5 mM⚠️ 1.08×❌ anti-selective
Colon lumen (dysbiotic)0 %100 mM❌ anti-selective❌ anti-selective

Results

The colon lumen is anoxic (0 % O₂) where the tumour core is merely hypoxic (0.5 %), so the hypoxia arm reads the lumen more strongly than the tumour in all three luminal scenarios. In dysbiosis both designed arms invert simultaneously, and by Eq. (18) no parameter choice whatsoever can repair this.

This bites harder than it looks, because §1.2 established that the gate is lactate-dominated — the arm that actually does the work is the one that fails under high luminal lactate.

The ceiling (Eq. (19)) says where the limit comes from:

Site $L_{\text{off}}$ Wild type $n_L{=}1$ $n_L{=}2$ $n_L{=}4$ $n_L$ needed for 10×
Lumen (healthy)0.6 mM2.28×13.3×178×31,605×0.89
Lumen (faecal)5 mM1.08×1.60×2.56×6.55×4.90
Lumen (dysbiotic)100 mM0.87×1.00×1.00×1.00×impossible

Those shape bounds are then truncated by the basal term: with wild-type $b_L=1/7$, $\min\{178,\,7\}=\mathbf{7.0\times}$.

It is the concentration ratio between the two sites and the basal level — not the sensor's midpoint — that set what is achievable. Wild-type lldPRD is capped at 7× however it is tuned, and reaching 10× against faecal lactate would need $n_L\ge4.9$ while LldR has no reported cooperativity.

What holds the lumen off is the part we chose. BBa_M36021 is the native lldPRD promoter, and it retains the native anoxic and glucose repressions that engineered variants were built to remove. The two environments differ in exactly those two respects:

Colon lumen Tumour core
Oxygenanoxic (0 %)hypoxic but not anoxic
Glucosedietary, proximally richdepleted (glycolysis)

The repressions engage where we need them and relax where we do not. With 0.1 residual activity each (100× combined):

Site Native (repressed) Engineered (de-repressed) Repression needed for 10×
Lumen (healthy)227.6×2.28×≥ 4.39×
Lumen (faecal)108.2×1.08×≥ 9.24×
Lumen (dysbiotic)86.9×0.87×≥ 11.51×

The worst case asks for about 11.5× combined, and the published characterisation of this promoter reports both repressions as complete.

That characterisation is the one we take $EC_{50}$ and the dynamic range from, so it is not a separate assumption. Rebuilding the wild-type lldPRD biosensor on a low-copy plasmid, the authors found no detectable response in the presence of 0.4 % glucose, and no response at all after 16 h under anaerobic conditions8 — the whole point of their engineering effort was to remove those two repressions, and the resulting ALPaGA promoter is a different part from the one we built. The native repressions are the documented behaviour of BBa_M36021 under exactly the two conditions the colon lumen imposes: glucose-rich and anoxic. LldR's control of the operon, and its loss of induction in an lldR deletion, are established separately19.

We nevertheless credit each repression with only 10×. A promoter that is "not detectably induced" in an assay with a finite floor could be repressed 10× or 10,000×, and the margin scales as $R_{\text{rep}}^{1/n_Q}$ (Eq. (12)), so the difference is worth at most a factor of 10 in the margin — but nothing below is allowed to depend on the generous reading.

Washout (Eq. (22)) contributes little: with $t_{1/2}^{\text{AHL}}=8$ h, suppression is 12.5× at 1 h transit but only 1.48× at 24 h — and colonic transit is slow, landing at the weak end. It is a secondary mechanism.

That 8 h is a declared placeholder, not a measurement, and we looked for one. The standard study of AHL lactonolysis reports only relative rates — on a scale where C8-HSL is 1, our signal 3-oxo-C6-HSL is 170 at 37 °C — together with the finding that the 3-oxo substitution destabilises the ring and that warming from 22 to 37 °C speeds its opening 2.4×20. No absolute half-life at pH 7 is given, so none can be cited. What the paper does establish is the direction: 3-oxo-C6-HSL sits near the unstable end of the AHL series, and the large intestine's pH of 6.5–7.5 (the paper's own table of body fluids) is in the range where hydrolysis proceeds. A shorter true half-life means more luminal decay and a larger safety margin, so the placeholder errs against us, and this section claims nothing from it either way.

🔴 Design consequence: do not "fix" this promoter. Swapping in a de-repressed variant to raise tumour expression would discard the only mechanism holding the lumen off — discrimination falls from 86.9–227.6× back to 0.87–2.28×, and the full gate from 23–60× to 0.23–0.60×. That is the difference between a margin and an inversion.

2.3.4 The one assumption that cannot fail quietly

Every other open parameter in this work widens an interval. This one inverts a conclusion, and it is a binary with no measurement behind it:
Assumptionthe colon lumen is anoxic (0 % O₂) and the tumour core (≈0.5 %) is not
Formbinary flag, not a fittable parameter
Measured halfat 1 % O₂ with lactate the circuit reaches its highest corner, 97.9 % positive ⇒ the promoter is plainly not repressed at 1 %, which is what the tumour side needs
Untested halfnothing in our dataset is at 0 % O₂
Failure modesign change, not a wider interval

Two things argue it holds: the requirement is modest (4.39× healthy, 9.24× faecal, 11.51× dysbiotic) against two repressions each reported as strong, and FNR-type oxygen regulation switches over exactly the 0–1 % range that separates the two sites. But modest and reported is not measured, and we would rather say so than let it pass as established.

One plate settles it: the reporter at 0 % against 1 % O₂, lldPRD-only.

2.4 SsrA as a post-translational valve

Question. Keep the degron or drop it — and what is the criterion? What is the effector's half-life in normal tissue? Is a second degron warranted? And is SsrA a sufficient safety valve or only an auxiliary one?

Model

Delivered exposure is biomass × per-cell potency, so dropping the tag multiplies potency by $r_{\text{potency}}$ and biomass by $r_{\text{biomass}}$:

$$\frac{\text{delivery(tagged)}}{\text{delivery(untagged)}} =\frac{1}{r_{\text{biomass}}\,r_{\text{potency}}}>1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_{\text{potency}}<r^{*}\equiv\frac{1}{r_{\text{biomass}}}$$
(23)

Keep the tag if and only if the potency it costs is less than the biomass it buys. This uses two measured ratios and assumes nothing about dose–response shape.

Treating degradation strength as a continuous knob:

$$P(\delta)=\frac{\delta_{\text{nat}}+\delta_{\text{built}}}{\delta_{\text{nat}}+\delta}, \quad \text{potency}=\frac{P}{k_{\text{export}}+P}, \quad \text{viability}=e^{-\lambda P}$$
(24)

Each of the latter two carries exactly one free parameter, matched to the two measured states — the identifiability ceiling of this dataset.

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{\delta_{\text{nat}}+\delta_{\text{tag}}}$$
(25)

Finally, ClpXP is a finite enzyme. Michaelis–Menten degradation gives an effective first-order rate that falls as the pool grows:

$$v=\frac{v_{\max}P}{K_m+P}, \qquad k_{\text{eff}}(P)=\frac{v_{\max}}{K_m+P}$$
(26)

so amplification exists only inside a capacity window:

$$\text{leak rate}\ <\ v_{\max}\ <\ \text{induced rate}$$
(27)

where

  • $r_{\text{biomass}}$ is the 24 h biomass ratio of the untagged strain to the tagged (1.380/2.360 = 0.585).
  • $r_{\text{potency}}$ is the per-cell potency ratio of the untagged strain to the tagged.
  • $r^{*}=1/r_{\text{biomass}}$ (1.71) is the decision threshold; keep the tag iff $r_{\text{potency}}<r^{*}$.
  • $P(\delta)$ is the normalised steady-state effector pool.
  • $\delta$ is the total effector degradation rate; $\delta_{\text{nat}}$ (0.08 h⁻¹) and $\delta_{\text{tag}}$ (0.43 h⁻¹ as built) are its natural and tag-added components.
  • $\text{potency}=P/(k_{\text{export}}+P)$ is the per-cell killing potency, and $k_{\text{export}}$ its half-saturation constant.
  • $\text{viability}=e^{-\lambda P}$ is the chassis survival fraction, and $\lambda$ the viability penalty coefficient.
  • $t_{1/2}=\ln2/(\delta_{\text{nat}}+\delta_{\text{tag}})$ is the effector half-life.
  • $v$ is the ClpXP degradation rate; $v_{\max}$ and $K_m$ are its maximum rate and Michaelis constant.
  • $k_{\text{eff}}(P)=v_{\max}/(K_m+P)$ is the effective first-order degradation rate at pool $P$.
  • leak rate and induced rate are the promoter leak and fully induced synthesis rates; amplification exists iff leak rate $<v_{\max}<$ induced rate.

Substituting

$$r_{\text{biomass}}=\frac{1.380}{2.360}=\mathbf{0.58475} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r^{*}=\mathbf{1.71014}$$
Dose untagged tagged $n$ $r_{\text{potency}}$ Margin $r^*/r$ Verdict
6 OD2.900 %3.267 %30.88781.926×✅ keep
8 OD7.150 %6.733 %2 ⚠️1.06191.610×✅ keep
10 OD22.333 %15.800 %31.41351.210×✅ keep

Calibrating Eq. (24)/4 on the most conservative anchor gives $\lambda=0.12265$, $k_{\text{export}}=0.56104$. Untagged pool from Eq. (24): $P(0)=0.43/0.08=\mathbf{5.375}$. Delivery at the built strength $\delta=0.35$: $P=1.000$, potency $=1/1.56104=0.6406$, viability $=e^{-0.12265}=0.8846$, so $0.5667$; untagged gives $0.4685$. Their ratio 1.2099× matches Eq. (23)'s $1/(0.58475\times1.4135)$ exactly — two independent routes agreeing.

Results

Keep the tag. All three doses satisfy $r<r^{*}$, with margins 1.21–1.93×. At the lowest dose $r<1$: the tagged construct actually kills slightly more. The 3.3× spread in potency cost we inherited was an artefact of pairing a numerator from one block with a denominator from another; the only legitimate value is 1.4135, so what was recorded as an open question is in fact settled. Had the rejected 4.6993 been used, Eq. (23) would give 0.364× and invert the decision.

Effector half-life in normal tissue (Eq. (25)):

Variant $\delta_{\text{total}}$ Half-life
Untagged0.08 h⁻¹8.66 h
SsrA as built0.43 h⁻¹1.61 h
Double SsrA (hypothetical)0.78 h⁻¹0.89 h

Both figures are declared rather than measured on our construct, so it is worth saying where they sit. The SsrA system's half-lives were characterised by appending the tag's last residues to GFP in E. coli: the variants span about 40 minutes to a few hours, set by the final three residues21. Our tagged value, 1.61 h (97 min), is inside that span, and the untagged 8.66 h is outside it on the stable side — which is what an untagged protein should be. Neither number is a measurement of GSDMD-N, and §2.4's conclusion does not need one: the decision is a ratio comparison (Eq. (23)), and §4.4 refits the exponent per construct rather than transporting a rate.

A second degron is not warranted. The tag as built is already 2.35× stronger than the delivery optimum ($\delta^*=0.149$ h⁻¹), at a cost of 7.34 % in delivered exposure — far below the cost of rebuilding and revalidating, and §2.4's amplification argument says over-strength helps on the safety side.

SsrA is a genuine safety valve, not an auxiliary — because ClpXP saturates. By Eq. (26), degradation is strong where the only substrate is promoter leak ($P\ll K_m$) and is outrun where the gate is open ($P\gg K_m$). The protein-level tumour/normal ratio therefore exceeds the promoter's transcription ratio: the degron amplifies selectivity rather than merely damping output. The same mechanism explains why over-strength is not a defect — a stronger tag pushes normal tissue deeper into the unsaturated regime.

⚠️ $v_{\max}$ and $K_m$ for EcN ClpXP on this substrate are unknown, so the amplification factors we can compute (peaking near 70.9× with demonstration parameters) are illustrative, not predictive. What this section reports is the structural requirement (Eq. (27)) — the same methodology as §2.3: when a parameter cannot be pinned down, state where it must lie.

A separate finding, from §3.1: about 88.5 % of the degron's spatial safety benefit comes from making less, not from confining what is made.

2.5 Which parameters decide the margin

Question. Across the declared ranges, which parameters dominate the variance of the bottleneck margin — and are they measurable?

Model

The tissue ratio is a product, so we analyse on a log scale, which turns Eq. (11) into a sum:

$$\log R_{\text{margin}}=\log\text{lac}+\log\text{hyp}+n_Q\log\frac{\text{hyp}}{d}+\log R_{\text{rep}}$$
(28)

A purely multiplicative model would then show zero interaction and first-order indices summing to 1. That makes the analysis diagnostic rather than merely descriptive: anything that survives is a real coupling. Eq. (28) contains exactly one — $n_Q$ multiplies $\log(\text{hyp}/d)$ — so we can predict in advance that $n_Q$ will carry a modest first-order index and a much larger total-order index.

$$S_i=\frac{V_i}{\mathrm{Var}[\log R_{\text{margin}}]}, \qquad S_{Ti}=1-\frac{V_{\sim i}}{\mathrm{Var}[\log R_{\text{margin}}]}$$
(29)

The gap between the two is what the parameter does through the others, so the share of a parameter's influence that is interaction is

$$\text{interaction share}_i=1-\frac{S_i}{S_{Ti}}$$
(30)

where

  • $R_{\text{margin}}$ is the bottleneck margin, the gate output at the limiting site.
  • $\text{lac}$, $\text{hyp}$ and $d$ are the lactate arm, hypoxia arm and luminal density ratio of Eq. (11).
  • $n_Q$ is the quorum Hill coefficient.
  • $R_{\text{rep}}=\rho_{\text{anox}}^{-1}\rho_{\text{glu}}^{-1}$ is the native-repression product.
  • $S_i$ and $S_{Ti}$ are the first- and total-order Sobol indices of parameter $i$, and $\text{interaction share}_i$ the part of $i$'s influence that acts through other parameters.
  • $V_i$ is the variance contribution of parameter $i$ and $V_{\sim i}$ the contribution of all the others.
  • $\mathrm{Var}[\log R_{\text{margin}}]$ is the total variance of the log margin.

$S_T\gg S_1$ marks a parameter that decides how much everything else matters.

Parameters

Nine parameters, each range carrying its own provenance; variance-based indices22 with the total-order estimator of23 as implemented in SALib24; Saltelli sampling, $n_{\text{base}}=1024$, second order off, 11,264 total samples, seed 20261008 (fixed, reproducible). Outputs: colonic mucosa, dysbiotic lumen, and the bottleneck = $\min_{\text{site}}R_{\text{margin}}$. The lactate ranges span both our published values and last cycle's generous ones, so the analysis covers the disagreement found in §2.1.

Results

The prediction holds (Eq. (30)):

Single sites are nearly additive (8–16 % residual), exactly as the log transform should produce. The bottleneck's 37.5 % residual is genuine: taking a minimum is a real nonlinearity, not an artefact of multiplying. And $n_Q$'s signature is as predicted — $S_T=0.2314$ against $S_1=0.0688$ at the bottleneck, a ratio of 3.4.

This explains §2.1 and §2.2 at once: both inherited wide ranges are $n_Q$ amplifying other uncertainties through a power law. A single-index analysis cannot see that structure.

For the colonic mucosa, oxygen-sensor affinity dominates ($S_1=0.5873$, $S_T=0.7365$), with the top three all oxygen parameters — independently confirming last cycle's finding. For the bottleneck the drivers are entirely different:

An analysis that stops at the mucosa is answering what drives a secondary site.

A self-consistency check: repression strength has an interaction share of 0.004, i.e. it is a pure additive term in Eq. (28) — exactly what a multiplicative repression factor should be. A large interaction there would have indicated an implementation error.

Why this page is computed at the published sensor values

The Sobol analysis names $K_{O_2}$ and $n_Q$ as the two parameters that decide the margin. Both were carried over from last cycle as declared priors. Both turn out to have published measurements behind them, and neither prior agreed with its measurement, so on 2026-10-14 we replaced them and recomputed the page. This subsection is the record of that change.

Oxygen affinity. The closest characterisation is an FNR-family (ANR) promoter run in an oxystat across the full range, which reports half-maximal induction at about $5\times10^{2}$ Pa and states that the dose response closely resembles the E. coli FNR-activated promoters10. Against the same paper's air reading of $210\times10^{2}$ Pa, that is

$$K_{O_2}=\frac{5\times10^{2}}{101325}\times100=\mathbf{0.49\ \%\ O_2}$$

against the inherited 1.0 %, which was never sourced to a measurement.

Quorum Hill coefficient. A single-cell study of a LuxI/LuxR sender–receiver pair fits the pLux dose response at four levels of resolution and gets $n=0.97\pm0.08$ in bulk, $0.95\pm0.2$ in a microfluidic chemostat, and $1.2\pm0.3$ to $1.5\pm0.6$ from single-cell trajectories; it also reports that earlier quantitative analyses of the AHL/pLux system "typically resulted in Hill exponents around $n=1$–$1.5$"11. The inherited 2.0 was above that whole range. We take the published centre, $n_Q=1$, and sweep 0.95–1.5.

What changed. Every headline number on this page moved, and all but one moved in our favour:

The bottleneck is larger, the lumen is more clearly off without the native repression, the density headroom triples, and the §3.5 collision — the worst result on this page — eases from "nothing left" to 4.4×. The one that shrinks is the lesion-size turn-on, which §2.2 already identified as an $n_Q$ artefact rather than a mechanism; the geometric floor it rests on, 178 µm, does not depend on either parameter and is unchanged.

Across the published span the requirement is met with room. Sweeping $n_Q$ over Ramalho's full range at Højberg's $K_{O_2}$:

$n_Q=0.95$ $n_Q=1.0$ $n_Q=1.05$ $n_Q=1.25$ $n_Q=1.5$
Bottleneck20.73×21.85×22.33×19.56×16.57×

The worst case is 16.57×, 1.7× the requirement. What moves across the span is which site is the weakest link, not whether the design passes.

Where it does fail. Pushing either parameter well outside its published range breaks it: at $K_{O_2}=2$ % the mucosa collapses to ≈2.9× at every $n_Q$, and at $n_Q=3$ the dysbiotic lumen falls to 6.13×. Both are far outside anything reported, but they are the directions to watch, and they are why §7 still ranks a pPepT dose–response and an exogenous-AHL dose–response highly: a measurement on our own parts would replace a transferred one.

A note on transfer. Neither measurement is on our construct. Ramalho's is a LuxI/LuxR pair in E. coli, which is the same regulator and promoter we use. Højberg's is an ANR promoter in Pseudomonas, which is a weaker transfer — same regulator family, different organism, and our promoter is pPepT specifically. We adopted it anyway because a measurement on a comparable part beats a declared value with no provenance, but it is the single assumption on this page we would most like to retire.

Where to spend effort. 81 % of the bottleneck variance sits on two parameters, and one of them is measurable in a day — the same 0 % vs 1 % O₂ comparison that §2.3.4 asks for. Luminal EcN density needs colonisation data we cannot generate this cycle; the closest that exists is the six-patient arm of1, where two participants had no tumour enrichment over normal colon§2.1. That is enough to say the parameter is real and not enough to narrow its range.

The lactate-prior dispute does not decide safety. All three lactate parameters sit below $S_T=0.02$ at the bottleneck, because luminal lactate saturates the arm under either prior.

3. Efficacy — what dose is required?

3.1 Intra-nodule coverage and leakage

Question. Of what is produced inside a nodule, how much is destroyed outside it? Split the degron's benefit into "makes less" and "spreads less". And is intra-nodule flatness a consequence of the diffusion lengths, as previously claimed?

Model

The fraction of production that is destroyed outside a lesion of radius $R$ has a closed form, with $g$ the exterior amplitude function of Eq. (37) and $\alpha=R/\lambda$:

$$E(R,\lambda)=\frac{3\,g(\alpha)(1+\alpha)e^{-\alpha}}{\alpha^{3}}$$
(31)
$$G_{\text{field}}(R,\lambda)=\frac{\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)}{\Psi_{\text{in}}(R;R)}$$
(32)
$$\begin{aligned} \text{total off-target reduction}&=\rho_{\text{pool}}\times\frac{E_{\text{untagged}}}{E_{\text{tagged}}}\\[4pt] \text{confinement share}&=\frac{\ln(\text{confinement})}{\ln(\text{total})} \end{aligned}$$
(33)

where

  • $E(R,\lambda)$ is the fraction of production destroyed outside a lesion of radius $R$.
  • $R$ is the lesion radius (µm) and $\lambda$ the screening length of the effector field (µm).
  • $\alpha=R/\lambda$ is the radius-to-screening-length ratio.
  • $g(\alpha)$ is the exterior amplitude function of Eq. (37).
  • $G_{\text{field}}(R,\lambda)$ is the core-to-rim ratio of the effector field inside the lesion.
  • $\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)$ is the normalised AHL at the lesion centre (Eq. (35)) and $\Psi_{\text{in}}(r;R)$ the normalised internal field (Eq. (36)).
  • $\rho_{\text{pool}}$ is the intracellular effector-pool ratio, untagged over tagged.
  • $E_{\text{untagged}}$ and $E_{\text{tagged}}$ are the outside-destroyed fractions of the two constructs.

The share is taken in logs because the two contributions compose multiplicatively. The closed form agrees with direct numerical integration to $10^{-4}$, which our tests check, so this section does not rest on hand algebra.

Results

At $R=400$ µm:

Species $\lambda$ $\lambda/R$ Destroyed outside Free-field core:rim $\lambda<R$?
Lactate5099 µm12.7599.77 %1.539✗
AHL3000 µm7.5099.36 %1.566✗
GSDMD-N (no SsrA)670.8 µm1.67791.10 %1.784✗
GSDMD-N (+SsrA)300 µm0.75073.16 %2.072✅

Both constructs leak heavily. The 671 → 300 µm change sounds categorical — from larger than the nodule to smaller — but per molecule it moves off-target exposure by only 1.245×:

$$\text{retention}=\frac{1-0.7316}{1-0.9110}=3.015\times, \qquad \text{confinement}=\frac{0.9110}{0.7316}=1.245\times$$
$$\text{total}=5.375\times1.245=\mathbf{6.693\times}, \qquad \text{confinement share}=\frac{\ln1.245}{\ln6.693}=\mathbf{11.5\ \%}$$

About 88.5 % of the degron's spatial safety benefit comes from making less, and only 11.5 % from confining what is made. The more quotable claim (retention improves 3.0×) is not the one that drives safety. This agrees with §2.4, where the degron's value also lands on suppressing the accumulated pool.

Intra-nodule flatness is a boundary condition, not a length scale. Last cycle attributed core:rim ratios of 1.011–1.021 to the diffusion lengths dwarfing the nodule. That attribution does not hold: under free diffusion into surrounding tissue with the same decay rate, the same parameters give graded fields of 1.54–2.07×. Even lactate, with $\lambda/R=12.75$, shows a 1.54× gradient. And the tagged effector's 300 µm range is shorter than the 400 µm nodule radius in any case, so its field should not be called a long-range average under any boundary condition.

What actually flattens the field is a bounded domain with rim washout. Both treatments are defensible — free field assumes equal decay inside and out, washout assumes a well-perfused rim carries effector away — and the truth sits between them, so we report both and do not pick. The therapeutic conclusion (flat coverage spares nothing, including the proliferating rim) survives; its justification changes from a scale argument to a boundary-condition argument.

3.2 Clustered micro-lesions

Question. The AHL diffusion length is ~3000 µm, far larger than any single lesion. Does a cluster of micro-lesions 1–2 mm apart share one signal pool and switch itself on? If so, how large must the cluster be — and is that still micrometastasis?

Model

The steady-state AHL equation is the screened (modified Helmholtz) form of the reaction–diffusion equation, whose spherically symmetric solutions are standard25:

$$D\nabla^2C-\delta C+q(\mathbf x)=0, \qquad \lambda=\sqrt{D/\delta},\ \ \alpha=R/\lambda,\ \ s=r/\lambda$$
(34)

Because LuxI sits under pPepT rather than under pLux, AHL production does not depend on AHL concentration. There is no autoinduction loop, so Eq. (34) is linear, superposition is exact, and an arbitrary three-dimensional arrangement of spherical sources is solved by summing closed-form single-sphere fields. We had planned a 2-D axisymmetric finite-difference solver; it is not needed, and the analytic result is more accurate, cheaper and easier to defend.

The same fact yields an architectural conclusion that was not previously stated: the quorum module is a colonised-volume integrator, not a bistable switch — no hysteresis, no sharp threshold, a graded response. This agrees with §2.2, where AHL integration carried 6.5× the weight of the hypoxia term.

Normalised to $q/\delta$, for a single uniformly producing sphere:

$$\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)=1-(1+\alpha)e^{-\alpha}$$
(35)
$$\Psi_{\text{in}}(r)=1-(1+\alpha)e^{-\alpha}\frac{\sinh s}{s},\quad r\le R$$
(36)
$$\Psi_{\text{out}}(r)=\lambda\,g(\alpha)\frac{e^{-r/\lambda}}{r}, \qquad g(\alpha)=\alpha e^{\alpha}-(1+\alpha)\sinh\alpha,\quad r\ge R$$
(37)

The two expressions match at $r=R$, and for small $\alpha$ the exterior field reduces to the screened (Yukawa) point-source kernel. Our tests verify by finite difference that both branches satisfy the PDE.

Cluster centre concentration and cooperation factor:

$$\Psi_{\text{cluster}}(i)=\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)+\sum_{j\ne i}\Psi_{\text{out}}(d_{ij}), \qquad \text{coop}=\frac{\Psi_{\text{cluster}}(i)}{\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)}$$
(38)

Absolute AHL depends on $\beta_Q/K_Q$, on which last cycle's two calibrations differ 27-fold, so we report no absolute concentration and issue no ON/OFF verdict. Instead we invert Eq. (35):

$$R_{\text{eq}}:\quad \Psi_{\text{centre}}(R_{\text{eq}})=\Psi_{\text{cluster}}$$
(39)

the equivalent isolated radius — the single lesion that would produce the same signal at its own centre. The threshold cancels, letting us compare directly against last cycle's 150 µm (OFF) → 1000 µm (ON) interval.

Finally, the small-$\alpha$ scaling that decides the dispersion question:

$$\underbrace{\Psi_{\text{centre}}\sim\frac{\alpha^2}{2}}_{\text{own}\ \propto\ R^2} \qquad\text{vs}\qquad \underbrace{\Psi_{\text{out}}\sim\frac{R^3}{3\lambda^2 d}}_{\text{neighbour}\ \propto\ R^3/d}$$
(40)

where

  • $C$ is the AHL concentration, $D$ its diffusion coefficient and $\delta$ its decay rate.
  • $q(\mathbf x)$ is the volumetric AHL production rate at position $\mathbf x$.
  • $\lambda=\sqrt{D/\delta}$ is the screening length.
  • $\alpha=R/\lambda$ and $s=r/\lambda$ are the radius and the radial position in screening-length units.
  • $\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)$ is the normalised AHL at a single lesion's centre (Eq. (35)), $\Psi_{\text{in}}(r)$ the normalised internal field (Eq. (36)) and $\Psi_{\text{out}}(r)$ the normalised exterior field (Eq. (37)).
  • $g(\alpha)$ is the exterior amplitude function of Eq. (37).
  • $\Psi_{\text{cluster}}(i)$ is the normalised AHL at the centre of lesion $i$ within a cluster.
  • $\text{coop}=\Psi_{\text{cluster}}(i)/\Psi_{\text{centre}}(R)$ is the cooperation factor.
  • $d_{ij}$ is the centre-to-centre distance between lesions $i$ and $j$.
  • $R_{\text{eq}}$ is the equivalent isolated radius: the single-lesion radius producing the same centre signal.

Substituting

$R=150$ µm, $\alpha=0.05$: $\Psi_{\text{centre}}=1-1.05\,e^{-0.05}=\mathbf{1.2091\times10^{-3}}$. $R=1000$ µm, $\alpha=1/3$: $\mathbf{4.4625\times10^{-2}}$.

Numerical note. Eq. (35) and $g(\alpha)$ cancel to second and third order respectively, so below $\alpha<0.01$ we switch to series expansions. The threshold must not be set higher: at $\alpha=0.05$ the closed form still carries ~12 significant digits while a four-term series carries 5.

Results

Spacing Lesions Cooperation Equivalent radius Reaches ON?

276.75×400.6 µm✗
12516.91×651.7 µm✗
1000 µm131.89×207.5 µm✗
1253.95×303.0 µm✗

No cluster reaches the 1000 µm equivalent. Cooperation is real but weak: at realistic micrometastatic spacing (≥ 1 mm), 125 lesions reach only 201–303 µm.

How large would it have to be?

Touching cluster Cooperation Equivalent radius Centre-to-centre span

$7^3=343$30.37×897.0 µm1.8 mm

512 touching 150 µm lesions is a contiguous mass 2.1 mm across (2.4 mm including the outer radii). That is no longer micrometastasis — it is a tumour, and the single-lesion model already says a tumour of that size switches on. The multi-lesion extension opens no new risk window.

That conclusion does not depend on the screening length

$\lambda=3000$ µm is inherited from last cycle's run manifest and is the least defensible number in this section: it is $\sqrt{D/\delta}$ built from an AHL diffusion coefficient and an AHL decay rate, neither of which we could source to a direct measurement (§2.3 says the same about the decay half). Published tumour-tissue diffusion coefficients for a small metabolite are of order $10^{-5}$ cm² s⁻¹26, which with an 8 h half-life puts $\lambda$ in the low millimetres — consistent with 3000 µm, but as a plausibility check, not a citation for the value.

So the honest move is to show the conclusion over a range rather than defend the point estimate. Across a ten-fold span of $\lambda$:

$\lambda$ $R_{\text{eq}}$ at 125 lesions $R_{\text{eq}}$ at 512 Lesions needed to reach 1000 µm
1000 µm608.4 µm888.7 µm1000
3000 µm (ours)651.7 µm1009.8 µm512
10000 µm665.9 µm1049.4 µm512

No value of $\lambda$ in that range lets a cluster reach the ON band at fewer than 512 lesions, and a shorter screening length makes it harder, not easier. The quantity the conclusion rests on is the count, and the count is bounded below across the whole span. That is why this section survives having its worst parameter undetermined, and it is the reason we report $\lambda$ as scenario rather than quietly treating 3000 µm as known.

And dispersion is strictly worse than compaction, confirming Eq. (40):

Lesions Equivalent radius (dispersed) Volume-matched single Ratio
4200.4 µm238.1 µm0.842
8251.0 µm300.0 µm0.837
27400.6 µm450.0 µm0.890
125651.7 µm750.0 µm0.869

Dispersing a given burden always produces less centre signal than compacting it (0.84–0.95×), because a lesion's own contribution scales as $R^2$ while a neighbour's scales as $R^3/d$.

Every modelling choice here is conservative in the same direction: steady state (transients fall below steady values), equal colonisation density across lesions (real micrometastases are probably colonised worse), no commensal lactonase degradation of AHL, and a lattice arrangement (which favours cooperation more than a random one).

For safety this strengthens the micro-lesion argument. For efficacy it says the circuit cannot clear true micrometastases, and distant disease has to be addressed immunologically rather than by colonisation — which §3.6 takes up.

3.3 Dosing: schedule versus persistence

Question. Can dosing schedule or inoculum size change cumulative exposure? If not, what is the actual lever?

Model

With a monomolecular approach to a fixed capacity (the shape §1.3 established), cumulative exposure over a window $T$ is

$$\int_0^{T}N\,dt=KT-(K-N_0)\frac{1-e^{-rT}}{r}$$
(41)

The inoculum enters only the second term, flattened by $1/r$. Against first-order clearance $k_{\text{clr}}$ competing with growth $\mu$:

$$K_{\text{eff}}=K\max\!\left(1-\frac{k_{\text{clr}}}{\mu},0\right), \qquad \text{exposure}=K_{\text{eff}}T$$
(42)

where

  • $N$ is the bacterial density and $T$ the exposure window (h).
  • $K$ is the carrying capacity and $N_0$ the inoculum density.
  • $r$ is the approach rate of the monomolecular law.
  • $k_{\text{clr}}$ is the first-order clearance rate and $\mu$ the growth rate.
  • $K_{\text{eff}}=K\max(1-k_{\text{clr}}/\mu,\,0)$ is the effective capacity under clearance.

Results

With $K=1.507$, $r=0.35$ h⁻¹, $T=168$ h, a 32-fold range of inoculum (0.005 → 0.16) moves exposure by 0.178 % — 248.885 to 249.327 — while onset time does shift, from 1.97 h to 1.66 h. The dose changes onset, not the integral.

The lever is persistence. At $\mu=0.60$ h⁻¹:

Clearance Plateau Exposure vs no clearance
0.00 h⁻¹1.507253.181.000
0.20 h⁻¹1.005168.780.667
0.55 h⁻¹0.12621.100.083
1.00 h⁻¹00eliminated

Clearance at 0.55 h⁻¹ cuts exposure to 8.3 %, and above the growth rate the colony is eliminated. Clearance is the dominant lever; dosing frequency is not.

⚠️ But the corollary that redosing adds nothing is circular. Our model contains no mechanism by which a colony can go extinct: growth is positive whenever the population is under capacity, there is no stochastic loss and no adaptive immunity. "Redosing merely reseeds an already-full niche" is therefore a property of how we built the model, not an inference from data. We have flagged it in code with three locked assertions (model_permits_extinction: False, conclusion_follows_from_construction: True, supported_by_data: False) so that it cannot be quoted as a result.

3.4 What dose is required

Question. What dose makes the kill rate match proliferation — in units we have actually realised? Is it inside the measured range, and does the extrapolation stay within the guard rail we declared?

Model

Step 1 — net dose–kill curve. Fitted in log–log after same-block, same-dose pairwise subtraction of a control:

$$f_{\text{net}}(d)=A\,d^{\,b} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \ln f_{\text{net}}=\ln A+b\ln d$$
(43)

Step 2 — efficacy criterion. A lesion is held when kill rate matches proliferation rate $r=\ln2/T_{\text{double}}$. Over a 24 h exposure this is closed form and assumes nothing about dose–response shape:

$$f_{\text{req}}=100\left(1-e^{-\ln2\cdot t_{\exp}/T_{\text{double}}}\right)\ \%$$
(44)

Step 3 — inversion.

$$d^{*}=\left(\frac{f_{\text{req}}}{A}\right)^{1/b}$$
(45)

Delivery loss and lesion-radius compensation follow as cube roots:

$$M_{\eta}=\eta^{-1/b}, \qquad M(R)=\left(\frac{G(R)}{G(R_{\text{ref}})}\right)^{-1/b}$$
(46)

where

  • $f_{\text{net}}(d)$ is the net killing fraction at dose $d$ (OD).
  • $A$ and $b$ are the amplitude and exponent of the dose–kill power law (0.02510 %/OD$^{b}$, 2.651).
  • $f_{\text{req}}$ is the required kill fraction, set by the exposure window $t_{\exp}$ (24 h) against the tumour volume doubling time $T_{\text{double}}$ (CT26 24–48 h; human CRC 100–600 d).
  • $d^{*}=(f_{\text{req}}/A)^{1/b}$ is the required dose.
  • $\eta$ is the fraction of effector retained inside a nodule (0.268), and $M_{\eta}=\eta^{-1/b}$ the dose multiplier for effector loss outside it.
  • $M(R)=[G(R)/G(R_{\text{ref}})]^{-1/b}$ is the dose multiplier for the reduced gate output at radius $R$, with $G(R_{\text{ref}})$ its value at the reference radius.

Our range brackets it, and the figure we quote is roughly twice as strict as that median, so the dose numbers below are not flattered by the choice.
